Beyond the Federal Floor: Why New York's Landfills Need Stronger Rules

Executive Summary

Right now, a New York landfill can burn nearly a billion cubic feet of landfill gas in a year and never be required to check its surface for leaks. That’s not a hypothetical. It happened at the Chemung County Landfill, operated by the waste company Casella in Elmira in 2024.

Welcome to the federal floor. Until New York finishes the landfill rules it is drafting, the state’s municipal solid waste (MSW) landfills follow this federal air standard. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) wrote it, last updated it in 2016, and built it on an honor system: operators check themselves, grade themselves, and report their own results.

The stakes are high. Landfills are the largest source of emissions in New York’s waste sector, which reported 14 percent of the state’s gross greenhouse gas emissions in 2023. Methane traps about 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in its first 20 years in the atmosphere. A toxic cocktail of pollutants like PFAs or forever chemicals, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, benzene, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) can escape from a landfill, all of which pose direct risks to the health of those living nearby as they are associated with severe and chronic health conditions like asthma, organ damage, and cancer, and can cause coughing, difficulty breathing and nausea. Children, the elderly, those experiencing racism and those with pre-existing health conditions are especially vulnerable to pollution from landfills.

What does an honor system look like when no one’s grading the test? We wanted to find out. So we obtained the state Department of Environmental Conservation’s (DEC) own compliance records for 16 of the largest New York municipal solid waste landfills through the Freedom of Information Law. Here’s what we found:

  • A threshold that never measures methane. Whether a landfill must meet federal gas control standards depends on a gas sample retaken only every five years, and that sample measures nonmethane organic compounds (NMOC), not methane. NMOC levels swing wildly. At the DANC landfill in upstate New York, six tests since 1996 ranged eightfold, from 46 to 372 parts per million, and each result locked in the landfill’s status for the next five years1. In 2021, EPA found DANC over the threshold, but its routine five-year sample came in lower, and DANC remains exempt today2. The large Chemung landfill stayed exempt through 2024 on a single 2019 sample3.

  • New trash left to vent pollution for years. Buried food waste starts turning into methane almost immediately, and half its food waste becomes landfill gas within about three and a half years. Yet federal rules let landfills wait up to five years to start capturing it. By then, much of that methane is already in the air. At High Acres landfill, no one checked a new section of the landfill for leaks for five years. The first check found methane at 41,000 parts per million (ppm) - 82 times the federal limit4.

  • Methane leaks that keep coming back. At five landfills, the same spots failed again and again. DEC flagged the repeat leaks at Seneca Meadows six times, and the federal rule gave it nothing to require but another rescan5.

  • Blind spots built into the map. At three landfills, 10% to a third of the surface went completely unchecked in a typical quarter6. When EPA inspectors showed up, they found leaks the operators’ own monitoring had missed7. At Modern Landfill, EPA measured leaks at about one in five points in a year when the operator reported none.8

  • Flares nobody tests. Chemung landfill burned its gas in open flares that federal rules won’t require to be tested, even after 2027, while that gas carried hydrogen sulfide at several times the level that deadens the sense of smell9. Near the Brookhaven landfill in Long Island, DEC inspectors smelled hydrogen sulfide off the property on 10 of 11 visits10.

None of this is unique to New York; it is what the flawed, loophole-ridden federal floor allows everywhere. But that rule is a floor, not a ceiling, and many states have upgraded. Proven fixes have been implemented in states like California, Colorado, and Maryland. Roughly 370 landfills, 70 percent of them publicly owned, already operate under updated state requirements. And DEC has started the process to upgrade its standards, holding its first stakeholder meeting in June 2026.

How to read this report. Each section follows the same four steps. The problem explains what the federal rule allows. Why it matters explains the consequence for emissions and for the people who live nearby. What we found in New York gives examples from files submitted by landfills to DEC, , each footnoted to the source document. The fix describes best practices or what other states already require and what New York’s rule should include.

Other States Upgraded. New York Is Stuck

Federal rules are outdated and flawed. Federal landfill air emissions regulations have failed to keep pace with technological and scientific advances. Every landfill in this report is regulated under the federal New Source Performance Standards (NSPS)/Emissions Guidelines (EG). Federal regulations rely heavily on self-reporting by the landfills, weak performance standards and limited oversight. This regulatory gap has discouraged the consistent use of available tools and technologies to better detect and repair methane leaks and effectively capture landfill gas. Chronic problems with landfill cover integrity, insufficient monitoring, and delayed installation of gas collection systems have enabled significant methane emissions and pollutants to escape.

The U.S. EPA’s own enforcement program has flagged widespread noncompliance at MSW landfills, concluding that many landfill operators are failing to conduct compliant methane leak monitoring and proper maintenance of gas collection and control systems (GCCS), problems that directly undermine pollution control. In New York, EPA’s own inspections at High Acres, Seneca Meadows, Ontario County, DANC and Modern Landfill11 found leaks or compliance problems that the operators’ records had missed (see sections 1 and 4).

New York’s municipal solid waste landfills are a major source of climate and air pollution, and one of the fastest places to cut it. The state’s 86 MSW landfills reported 4.8 million metric tons of CO2-equivalent from methane in 2023 (20-year basis) according to the Greenhouse Gas Reporting program. That figure is an undercount. Fewer than a third of New York’s MSW landfills were required to report their methane to EPA, and the reported numbers rest on modeled estimates rather than measurement. Aircraft and satellite surveys have found large methane plumes above more than half of the landfills observed nationally.

Without new rules, the problem grows. Full Circle Future’s modeling of New York’s landfills estimates that their actual methane emissions in 2023 were about six times what was reported to EPA, and projects that under current policies they will emit more than 10 million metric tons of methane between 2025 and 2050 (about 812 million metric tons CO2e, 20-year basis). Stronger landfill rules, with earlier and more complete gas collection, better cover and modern leak detection, could cut that by 46 percent: about 4.7 million metric tons of methane, or 371 million metric tons CO2e (20-year basis). That is equal to taking more than 80 million cars off the road every year.

Other states have already acted. The EPA sets the floor, not the ceiling, when it comes to state landfill air emission regulations. Other states aren’t waiting. EPA sets the floor, not the ceiling, and six states have already raised the bar. Roughly 370 landfills, 70 percent of them publicly owned, already meet more effective state standards. For example, Colorado’s Regulation 31, adopted in December 2025, requires more landfills to collect their gas, uses satellites and aircraft to find big leaks, phases out open flares, and makes companies that receive landfill gas share responsibility for compliance. Colorado expects it to cut up to 12.53 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2050. Washington, Oregon, Maryland, and Michigan have stronger rules, too, and California strengthened its long-standing rules in November 2025 to find and fix leaks faster, crack down on repeat problems, and put methane detection data in public view.

New York has a chance to close this gap right now, by following other states and upgrading its landfill standards. On June 4, 2026, the DEC held a pre-rulemaking stakeholder meeting on amendments to cut greenhouse gas emissions from New York’s landfills. The records in this report show where the federal floor is failing in New York, and point to the upgrades that New York’s rule needs.

1. The Loophole That Let a Billion Cubic Feet of Gas Go Unmonitored

The problem: Federal rules set minimum standards for landfill gas collection: wells where the gas is, systems that actually pull it in, regular checks of the surface for leaks, and deadlines to fix them. But a landfill doesn’t have to meet any of those standards until it clears two federal bars. Until then, methane and toxic pollutants like benzene can seep into the air, and no one is required to stop them, or even look. First, it must be permitted to hold at least about 2.75 million tons of waste (2.5 million metric tons). Second, a calculated estimate of its nonmethane organic compounds (NMOC), the smog-forming and toxic gases in landfill gas such as benzene and vinyl chloride, must exceed 34 metric tons a year. That estimate rests on a single round of gas sampling that only has to be repeated every five years. Until the next test, the landfill’s status is effectively locked in, no matter how much gas it is producing.

Why it matters: The federal rule has never measured methane, the pollutant landfills emit most and that is one of the most potent. Instead, it relies on an emissions rate for non-methane organic compounds (NMOC) coming from landfills, designed capacity that only includes massive landfills over 2.5 million tons of waste using a five-year snapshot. The result: A landfill can generate enormous amounts of methane and still fall below the federal threshold. States that have updated their rules, like Washington, Maryland, and California, fixed this: they decide which landfills need gas controls based on how much methane their waste actually generates, recalculated every year.

What we found in New York:

Chemung County Landfill: Too big to be a close call: Chemung County Landfill, near the Pennsylvania border, burned nearly a billion cubic feet of landfill gas in 2024. The landfill, owned by Chemung County and operated by Casella Waste Systems, collected 968 million cubic feet of gas that year, almost 46 percent of it methane, and burned all of it in two open flares, a process that releases hazardous pollutants like volatile organic compounds (VOCS) and particulate matter into the air.12 Chemung is not a borderline case in size. EPA's greenhouse gas reporting puts its design capacity at about 9.1 million metric tons, more than three and a half times the federal size cutoff, and it already holds about 6.5 million tons of waste.13

Photo of a landfill to come

About 15,400 people live within 5 miles of Chemung County Landfill. More than a quarter are low-income, one in five is over 64, and adults have COPD at about 1.6 times the state rate. All of them already live with fine-particle air pollution worse than 90% of New York.

One sample, five years of exemption. Yet a single gas sample from May 2019 kept Chemung below the federal threshold for gas collection and control every year through 2024. Between tests, the operator simply updates its waste tonnage and reuses the old sample.14 15 When Chemung finally retested in May 2024, it came in over the NMOC federal limit.16 Even then, the federal rule gives it until January 1, 2027, to comply.17

Chemung holds more than 6.4 million tons of trash, or the weight of nearly 18 Empire State Buildings. Yet its record shows no surface leaks, because no one was required to look.. It does have a gas collection system. The problem is that it doesn’t have to meet any of the federal standards to ensure it is operating properly: no requirements for where its wells go or how well they work, and no one required to walk the surface to find leaks or fix them by a deadline. Its state permit asks only for monthly pressure checks at its wells and daily visual checks of its flares (it’s really bad news when flares stop working).18

Under updated state rules, Chemung wouldn’t have been a close call. Based on the gas it reported collecting, its methane output is roughly 17 times the level at which California and Washington require gas controls, controls that come with real operating and monitoring standards.19 20

A large landfill with no federal controls. A single gas test can decide whether a landfill has to control its pollution at all, and the Development Authority of the North Country (DANC) landfill in Rodman, Jefferson County, shows how much rides on it. Because of how its tests came out, DANC still faces no federal requirement to check its surface for leaks, meet standards for its gas wells, or fix problems by a deadline. And DANC is no small operation. The publicly owned landfill has been open since 1992 and expects to keep accepting trash until 2074. It is designed to hold more than 21 million metric tons of waste - more than eight times the federal size cutoff - and already holds 6.7 million. In 2023, its estimated methane emissions reported to the EPA came to about 152,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent

DANC has run the same site-specific NMOC test six times since 1996. The results, in parts per million, were 129 in 1996, 372 in 2001, 46 in 2006, 80 in 2011, 202 in 2016 and 67 in 2021.21 Those six results come from the same landfill, measured the same way, five years apart. They range from 46 to 372 parts per million, an eightfold difference, and each one sets the landfill’s regulatory status for the next five years. A measure that swings this widely from one test to the next cannot reliably decide whether a landfill is regulated at all. And at DANC, the calculation had a second problem.

EPA caught DANC landfill undercounting its waste. A new sample let it off the hook. After an October 2020 inspection, EPA found that DANC had been subtracting large amounts of waste from its calculations as nondegradable without the documentation the federal rule requires. Recalculating with that waste included, EPA concluded in September 2021 that the landfill had actually crossed the 34-megagram threshold in 2020 and “became subject to NMOC control requirements as of December 31, 2020.”22

However, the timing worked in DANC’s favor. A month before EPA’s letter, DANC had already run its next five-year test, and the result, 67 parts per million, was a third of the 2016 reading. DEC approved it in October 2021. With the new number plugged in, DANC’s calculated emissions for 2024 were 13.89 megagrams, about 40 percent of the threshold, and its consultant reported that no further action was required. DANC still has no federal requirement to control its gas or monitor its surface, and its next test is not due until 2026.23

The federal rule allows exactly this. A landfill over the threshold must install controls “unless Tier 2 or 3 sampling demonstrates that the NMOC emission rate is less than 34 megagrams per year.”24 At DANC, a new sample taken a month before EPA found the landfill over the threshold was enough to put it back under.

Mill Seat: Methane in the air before the rules applied. Mill Seat’s February 2021 emissions report put it over the federal threshold for gas controls, but its 2021 compliance reports state that the federal operating requirements, which include surface monitoring, did not yet apply; its first quarterly surface scan came in early 2022.25 In between, in August 2021, an airborne survey detected two methane plumes over the landfill.

The fix: States that have updated their landfill rules have replaced the federal formula with what actually drives methane: how much waste is in the ground and how much methane it generates, recalculated every year. California, Washington and Maryland apply their rules to landfills with 450,000 tons of waste or more, and Oregon to landfills with more than 200,000 tons. Each then decides whether a landfill needs gas controls based on how much methane its waste generates, recalculated every year. Once a landfill’s methane crosses the trigger, the question becomes simple: is it leaking? If surface checks find methane at 200 ppm or higher at any point over four straight quarters, it must install a gas collection system that meets state standards, including quarterly leak checks. Only a landfill that proves it isn’t leaking can skip that step. Either way, someone has to look.

2. Gas Collection Installation and Methane Detection: The Five-Year Exemption

The problem: Methane starts forming soon after waste is buried, but federal rules let landfills wait up to five years before connecting a new area of waste to the gas collection system (two years if the area is closed or at final grade). And the same five-year clock means no one has to check whether new areas are leaking, even if gas collection pipes are already in the ground. Right now, by the time the pipes go in, much of the gas is already gone. EPA estimates that 61 percent of the methane from landfilled food waste is never captured, and that food waste is responsible for about 58 percent of all the methane escaping from U.S. landfills. As EPA itself put it, earlier gas collection “could collect and control significant emissions” from that fast-rotting food waste.

Why it matters: The lack of gas collection systems in the very place where there is the most pollution represents a systemic flaw in standards for landfills: gas collection begins only after the period of peak methane generation has already passed. Leak detection lags just as far behind. Federal rules don’t require surface emissions monitoring, or the walking surveys that find methane escaping through the landfill surface, in active areas until the waste there is five years old. That means the newest areas, where emissions are often highest, go unchecked, even when gas wells are already in the ground. These lag times are among the biggest missed opportunities in landfill methane mitigation.

What we found in New York:

Seneca Meadows: Five years of new waste, never checked. At Seneca Meadows, stage 6 of the landfill’s expansion was scheduled to begin receiving waste in 2018. Waste Connections, the landfill operator and one of the largest landfill companies in the U.S. knew it would produce gas: it planned dozens of gas wells and installed 28 in 2020.26 But the federal rule doesn’t require anyone to actually monitor for methane leaks on the surface until the waste is five years old, whether or not wells are in place. Those early years are exactly when landfills produce much of their methane. According to the EPA, half the carbon in landfilled food waste breaks down into landfill gas within 3.6 years, and those emissions “often occur before landfill gas collection systems are installed or expanded.” That means stage 6 was not scanned until September 2023, five years after filling was scheduled to begin. On that first scan, 13 locations exceeded the federal limit, two of them at 10,000 ppm: 20 times the limit, and as high as the instrument could read. 27

At High Acres Landfill, on the eastern edge of Monroe County, owned and operated by the largest landfill company in the country, WM, Cell 12 began receiving waste in January 2018 but was not monitored until February 2023, once its waste passed the five-year mark. On that first scan, at least 13 locations exceeded the federal limit, the highest at 41,000 ppm, 82 times the limit, and five of them triggered the federal 120-day repair process for persistent leaks and had to be fitted with new gas collection within 120 days.28 Both areas went years without a single surface reading, and both failed the first time anyone looked.

3. Gas Collection System Operations: Leaks Linger

The problem: When a spot on the landfill surface reads 500 parts per million (ppm) of methane or more, federal rules require the operator to make repairs (ie., amend the soil cover or adjust the gas extraction system) and check it again within 10 days. If the same spot fails three times in one quarter, the operator must install a new well or other collection device within 120 days, or get approval for an “alternative remedy.”29The rule has two gaps.

  • Chronic leaks never trigger a real repair: The rule counts failures one quarter at a time: a location that passes its follow-up checks starts the next quarter with a clean slate, no matter how many times it has failed before.

  • Quick patches stand in for real repairs. The rule’s own examples are real upgrades, like a bigger blower or new pipes. In practice, operators often propose adjusting the vacuum or adding more soil, which are the same steps that didn’t work the first time. Second, the rule’s own examples of alternative remedies are system upgrades, such as a larger blower or new header pipes, but nothing stops routine fixes from being approved instead. In practice, an alternative remedy often means adjusting the vacuum or adding additional cover soil, the same steps already tried in the first 10 days. Nothing in the federal rule treats a location that keeps failing as a sign of a bigger problem.

Why it matters: Neighbors breathe what escapes from a landfill. Our analysis of New York landfills found that half sit near communities with significantly higher asthma rates than the state average, and more than half sit near communities with unusually high shares of children under five. Methane leaks that keep coming back point to real infrastructure failures: wells that can’t hold vacuum, cover that won’t stay sealed, or collection systems too small for the gas the waste is producing. Under the current rule, those failures get the same treatment as a one-time leak, quarter after quarter.

What we found in New York: The records from four landfills show the same problem from four angles:

  • Mill Seat (Town of Riga, Monroe County): 16 leaks at once. At this county-owned landfill, permitted to keep taking trash until 2057, 16 spots were leaking at once in late 2024, nine of the 16 repaired spots leaked again.

  • High Acres (Perinton, near Fairport): the same problem wells, two years running. Neighbors here logged 4,604 odor complaints in 2020 alone. The same gas collection wells kept landing back on the repair list for two years.

  • Seneca Meadows (Waterloo and Seneca Falls): Six times, the DEC flagged repeat leaks here. Six times, it approved the same routine fix. If a fix hasn’t stopped the leaks, why keep approving it? More than 11,000 people live near New York’s largest active landfill, and they already face higher exposure to hazardous releases than 90 percent of the state.

  • Modern Landfill (Model City, Niagara County): leaks that never made the list. EPA found three risers leaking in 2023, a year when Modern’s own surveys reported no leaks at all. A year later the same three were leaking far worse.

Put side by side, these records show a system built to document leaks, not end them. A spot leaks, gets a quick patch, passes a recheck, and starts over, quarter after quarter, sometimes for years. Deadlines get pushed back. Regulators can flag the pattern but can require nothing more than another scan. Compliance reports can say “no deviations” while the leaks keep coming back. And through it all, the people living nearby keep breathing what escapes.

Mill Seat: Fixed, failed, and fixed again. In November 2024, 16 locations at Mill Seat failed three times in a single quarter. That set 16 simultaneous 120-day deadlines. The operator asked DEC for more time on nine, citing frozen and snow-covered ground, and DEC moved the deadline for the other seven to May 3, 2025, six months after the first failure.30 Several of the repaired spots failed again. A new vacuum line went in at MISOT135 in March 2025, and it was back on the 120-day list in the fourth quarter of 2025. Two wells that were to be linked by a new horizontal collector in early 2025 were both back on the list by the third quarter. Since 2024, every one of the Stage 5B vertical wells numbered 01 through 10 has been on a 120-day list at least once.31 This is what “fixed” looks like under the federal floor: a repair, a new deadline, and the same spot leaking again months later.

High Acres: The same wells keep leaking, and the rule never asks why. Between February 2023 and September 2025, High Acres issued 71 120-day notices on persistent methane leaks covering 53 locations. Thirteen locations appeared more than once, most of them in Cell 12, the area that failed its first scan in 2023. One Cell 12 well, was on the list four times in two years. Two others first failed in February 2023, on the first scan to cover Cell 12, and were still on the list in mid-2025.32 The count resets every quarter. In early 2024, no High Acres location went on the 120-day list at all, yet the repeat wells were still leaking: One read 12,000 ppm, 24 times the federal limit, and three others were over 1,000 ppm. In late 2025, a well already on the list three times read 8,613 ppm, more than 17 times the limit.33

Seneca Meadows: the regulator sees the problem, and approves the same inadequate fixes anyway. Between February 2024 and June 2025, DEC approved Seneca Meadows’ proposed fixes for 120-day locations where there were persistent leaks six times. Every approval letter included the same sentence: “There is a concern that corrective actions for repeat areas of exceedances may require additional follow-up between surface scan events.” Every one asked only for rescans.34 Every approval letter included the same sentence: ‘There is a concern that corrective actions for repeat areas of exceedances may require additional follow-up between surface scan events.’

Patches instead of real fixes: The repeats kept coming back. The first letter named three spots that had failed in back-to-back quarters. Every letter asked only that the fixed areas be rescanned over the next two quarters, and none required new collection equipment or an investigation of why the same spots kept failing. A spot on the Southeast Landfill, grid 2228, went on the 120-day list in mid-2023, was named by DEC as a repeat in early 2024, and was back on the list in the third quarter of 2024. It read over 500 ppm in six quarters, twice at the instrument’s 10,000 ppm maximum. Three wells in the Northwest Expansion were on the list in back-to-back quarters in late 2024 and early 2025. Both times the fixes were vacuum adjustments and cover soil, with bentonite or compaction, approved as alternative remedies in place of new collection equipment.35 When DEC’s requested rescans came in, all three were over 500 ppm again by September 2025. The first record of new collection equipment at these wells came in the third quarter of 2025, two years after one of them failed the area’s first scan.36

Modern Landfill (Model City, Niagara County): leaks that never made the list. In 2023, EPA found three risers venting gas at up to 13,400 ppm, in a year when Modern’s own surveys reported no exceedances, so the 120-day clock never started. Modern patched them; a year later EPA found the same three leaking at up to 112,000 ppm37 (see Section 4).Some wells could not collect gas at all: one had been raised with more than 100 feet of solid pipe and no openings.38 DEC confirmed landfill gas odors off-site on 13 days in late 2023 and required 17 new wells.39

The fix:

  • When a leak keeps coming back, the response has to escalate. California’s updated rule doesn’t let a problem area start over every quarter. If one monitoring area has five methane exceedances within 12 months, the operator has 30 days to inspect both the gas collection system and the landfill cover in that area and the areas around it. It then has 60 days to fix whatever is causing the leaks. Monitoring in that area increases from quarterly to monthly, and it stays monthly until six months in a row come back clean.

  • Finding the cause, not just patching the symptom. California applies the same logic to gas wells. A well with three pressure problems in a year triggers an inspection of the surrounding system and weekly checks for a full year.

  • Real-time monitoring: continuous vacuum and pressure monitoring, and monthly gas readings at every well.

  • Automated tuning where problems persist: Require sensors and valves that adjust each well in real time, required at landfills with persistent violations. These systems can increase methane recovery 10–20 percent.

  • Firm deadlines: Maryland, for example, requires corrective action within three days.

4. Methane Monitoring: What the Surveys Don't Cover

The problem:

The federal surface emissions monitoring (SEM) method that landfills are required to follow, known as Method 21, is labor-intensive, incomplete and prone to human error. It requires a technician to walk the landfill once per quarter along paths 100 feet apart - a full basketball court’s length -holding a handheld methane sensing device just above the ground. And incredibly, federal rules don’t require operators to show where they actually walked or to report every reading - only the spots that exceed the limit. That makes it nearly impossible to verify that the monitoring happened as required.

Worse, operators largely decide for themselves what to skip. The federal rule simply says “areas with steep slopes or other dangerous areas may be excluded” and it doesn’t spell out who decides or require any proof. EPA’s own 2024 enforcement alert flagged the “improper exclusion of areas from monitoring” as a recurring problem. EPA’s September 2024 nationwide enforcement alert found “widespread” compliance failures in monitoring: technicians moving too quickly, improperly excluding areas from monitoring, using expired calibration gases, and failing to fully inspect their work. Research shows that 60-79% of all landfill methane comes from the active working face, yet this area is typically exempt from SEM entirely. The result is an outdated honor system that lets methane slip by unnoticed: drones and aircraft have already spotted large clouds of methane rising from the very areas these surveys leave out.

Why it matters: You can’t fix a leak no one looks for. And the areas left off the map are often the leakiest. Active working face, where fresh trash is dumped, is a major source of landfill methane, yet it is typically exempt from leak checks. When researchers tested the federally approved walking survey at 10 landfills, it missed more than 80 percent of the methane. A clean monitoring record can simply mean no one checked.

What we found in New York: No one can say how much of these landfills was actually checked. For 12 of the 15 landfills we reviewed, the records don’t show which parts of the surface were checked for methane leaks and which were skipped. Only three, Seneca Meadows, Mill Seat, and High Acres, kept tables or maps detailed enough to tell. Even then, we had to measure the skipped areas on the operators’ maps ourselves. What we found at those three is striking. In a typical quarter, up to a third of the landfill’s surface went unchecked.

Seneca Meadows. a whole section never checked. Seneca Meadows, in Waterloo and Seneca Falls, is New York’s largest active landfill, taking in thousands of tons of trash a day, including from New York City. One part of the landfill’s Northwest Expansion, marked “NON-NSPS AREA” on the operator’s own map, was never monitored for methane exceedances in any quarter from 2022 to 2025 roughly 120 to 135 grid squares. Across the rest of the landfill, a fifth to nearly a third of grid squares were skipped each quarter in 2022 and early 2023, and about a tenth each quarter since.40

Mill Seat. a blind spot that keeps growing. Mill Seat landfill in the Town of Riga outside Rochester, covers a permitted footprint of nearly 217 acres and is permitted to keep taking trash until 2057. That area grew from 26 acres to 44 - up to a fifth of the landfill.41 Every quarterly map from 2023 through 2025 shades between 26 and 44 acres as either “not yet subject to surface monitoring (waste < 5 years old)” or “active / unsafe to traverse.” That is 12 to 20 percent of the landfill’s 216.9-acre permitted footprint, and the excluded area grew over the period.42

High Acres.: up to 46 acres, or 35 football fields, unmonitored. High Acres, in Perinton near Fairport, is cleared to take more than a million tons of trash a year, and its neighbors logged 4,604 odor complaints in 2020 alone. WM’s quarterly maps mark between 25 and 46 acres as either too new for federal monitoring or “unsafe to traverse” - as much as a fifth of the landfill’s constructed area, or roughly 35 football fields.43

Brookhaven: “not monitored due to safety concerns.” The Brookhaven landfill on Long Island sits beside North Bellport, a predominantly Black and Latino community with some of Long Island’s highest asthma rates and shortest life expectancies, and just two miles from an intermediate school. In the first quarter of 2024, 63 of the 875 points on the landfill’s walking route were skipped for “safety” reasons. And the gas collection plan Brookhaven submitted to EPA under a federal court settlement proposes skipping steep slopes, roads, active areas, truck traffic areas, and snow-covered ground altogether.44

Reduced monitoring leaves bigger gaps - more than half the route skipped equals a “clean” report. At the county landfill outside Binghamton, closed sections are checked for leaks only once a year. On that single scan in June 2023, 272 of the 514 points on one route or 53 percent were marked “area not monitored, active construction area.” The report still concluded there were no exceedances “over the area surveyed45

“Nothing found,” until the EPA looked: At Ontario County Landfill the county-owned site near Geneva and Seneca Lake operated by Casella, DEC had approved cutting leak checks on a closed section from four times a year to once. The operator’s 2023 annual scan found nothing over the limit. When EPA inspected in June 2024, it found five spots over the limit, including one at 2,292 ppm, more than four times the limit, filmed methane escaping from a pipe on infrared video, and called the monitoring program noncompliant. The section went back to quarterly checks.46 Brookhaven’s settlement with EPA likewise moved part of its landfill from annual back to quarterly checks.47 And some landfills aren’t checked at all: DANC, and Chemung until 2027. Landfills get no surface monitoring at all: DANC, and Chemung until 2027 (Section 1).

Modern Landfill: zero on paper, one in five in the field. Scanning alongside Modern’s staff in 2023, EPA found leaks at 18 of 84 points; Modern’s own quarterly surveys reported none all year. In 2024, EPA found 19 leaks at 94 points; Modern reported 11 for the year. EPA said Modern’s records “significantly underreport” leaks and called its monitoring noncompliant48. From above, the picture matched. Aircraft and satellites detected methane plumes from the same part of Modern’s landfill in 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025. One, on July 28, 2024, was estimated at about 1,400 kilograms of methane an hour, ten days before EPA’s inspection, in a quarter when Modern reported three exceedances49.

Independent checks find what federal walking surveys miss. In a two-day audit in August 2023, EPA found 22 locations over the federal methane limit at High Acres; 20 of them were not among the locations the operator’s scan three months earlier had found over even 200 ppm. At Seneca Meadows the same month, EPA found 20 exceedances, 11 of them in the Northwest Expansion, two weeks before the operator’s own program walked Stage 6 for the first time.50 And when High Acres’ Cell 12 and Seneca’s Stage 6 finally entered monitoring, at least 13 locations had measurements above the limit on the first monitoring walk (Section 2).

The fix: Check the whole landfill, with tools that can actually see it.

  • End the blind spots. Remove monitoring exemptions for the active working face and for areas deemed “unsafe” to walk. Research shows 60 to 79 percent of landfill methane comes from the working face, yet it’s usually excluded entirely.

  • Require full-surface monitoring with modern tools. DEC already has a precedent: its 2022 consent order with Ontario County requires quarterly surface monitoring of the areas the federal rule doesn’t cover, though those results are left out of the operator’s federal reports51. Drones, laser scanners, and fixed sensors can survey the entire landfill, including slopes and hazardous areas a technician on foot can’t safely reach. California’s updated rule already requires tools like handheld or drone-mounted laser scanners in areas that used to be skipped. Maryland, Oregon and Washington’s rules tighten walking surveys to 25-foot spacing.

  • Monitor more often, and in the right conditions. Quarterly walks miss leaks that come and go. Monitoring should be more frequent and happen under weather conditions that reflect real emissions, without high winds.

  • Add fenceline monitoring. Sensors around the landfill’s edge flag big leaks fast and measure pollution where it leaves the site and reaches nearby communities.

  • Make monitoring verifiable. Require GPS tracks of every survey, results for every grid (not just failures), and data in mapped, standardized formats. That way, regulators and the public can see what was checked and what was skipped.

  • Respond when satellites or aircraft spot a plume. California’s 2025 rule requires operators to inspect a 600-by-600-foot area around a detected plume within five days; Colorado’s rule requires operators to investigate, address, and report back on large releases. At High Acres, a satellite detected a methane plume in March 2026, spreading several kilometers downwind; no rule required anyone to investigate it.

5. Burning Gas With No Verification

The problem: Federal rules fall short on landfill flares in three ways:

  1. They allow open flares, which let methane and toxic pollution escape. About two-thirds of landfill flares in the U.S. are open “candlestick” flares, which is a pipe with a flame on top, exposed to wind and weather. Federal rules don’t require enclosed flares. An open flare only has to meet design specs, like no visible smoke and a lit pilot flame, and it is never tested.52

  2. They set a lower bar, allowing pollutants to escape. Enclosed control devices must cut 98 percent of nonmethane organic compounds (or meet a concentration limit) - a standard that doesn’t measure methane at all. Many states have upgraded to 99 percent methane destruction from every device. And for open flares, even the efficiency often claimed for them “is a design number on paper, not a verified field result”: real-world testing shows they often fall below 90 percent in wind or when gas flow changes.

  3. They ignore PFAS. Landfill gas also carries PFAS, the “forever chemicals.” A nationwide study of 30 landfills estimated that about 836 kilograms of PFAS escape U.S. landfills each year in uncollected gas - roughly as much as leaves through leachate, the polluted liquid that drains out of landfills.53 EPA says heat can destroy PFAS only under carefully controlled, high-temperature conditions, confirmed by testing.54 Yet nothing in the federal rule requires landfills to measure PFAS or prove their flares destroy it, and an open flare controls neither its temperature nor how long gas stays in the flame. None of the New York records we reviewed measured PFAS in landfill gas at all, before or after the flare.55

Why it matters: Whatever the flare doesn’t destroy, neighbors breathe: Forever chemicals, hydrogen sulfide, benzene, vinyl chloride, and other toxic compounds. Poorly performing flares are also a known source of the odors that drive community complaints. And open flares are an eyesore: a flame burning out in the open, around the clock, where enclosed flares keep it hidden inside a stack. And because federal rules require only occasional checks, a flare can run below par for months without anyone noticing.

What we found in New York: Chemung County, the county-owned landfill near the Pennsylvania border sits among neighbors already carrying a heavy health burden. Nearby adults have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) at a rate of 9.5 percent, compared with 6 percent statewide; the area has more young children and older adults than the state average; and more than 15,000 people living nearby already breathe fine-particle pollution at levels higher than 90 percent of the state. Chemung County landfill sent nearly a billion cubic feet of landfill gas through two open candlestick flares in 2024, with no enclosed flare and no energy recovery.56 Samples taken at one flare in December 2024 found 42% methane and hydrogen sulfide at 696 to 749 ppm,57 several times the 100 to 150 ppm at which, according to OSHA, hydrogen sulfide deadens the sense of smell.58 Based on the facility’s own gas volume and those readings, the flares would produce roughly 50 to 55 metric tons of sulfur dioxide a year.59

At Brookhaven, the town-owned landfill on Long Island sits beside North Bellport, a predominantly Black and Latino community. More than 120,000 people living near the landfill already breathe fine-particle pollution at levels higher than 90 percent of the state, and the area’s life expectancy is shorter than the state average. An enclosed flare has been the landfill’s main combustion device since January 2021, and it has never been tested to measure how much methane and other pollutants it actually destroys.. The Town’s latest compliance certification, filed in January 2026, still relies on a 2004 test of the previous flare, which is now disconnected. This is the same community where DEC inspectors detected hydrogen sulfide odors off the landfill property on 10 of 11 visits in December 2018.60

In both places, combustion performance is assumed, not verified.

The fix: The answer is simple: burn landfill gas in equipment that can be tested, then test it. Other states already do. Colorado, Washington, Maryland and California phase-out open flares and require enclosed flares at 99% destruction efficiency, with annual testing. In addition, New York’s rule should require PFAS measurement in landfill gas before and after the control device, so that what reaches nearby communities is known.

6. Transparency and Accountability: The Compliance Record That Doesn’t Show What the Data Shows

The problem: Every Title V landfill reports its compliance to DEC in a table of permit conditions, each with a yes-or-no answer: were there any deviations? That column is what a reviewer, or a member of the public, sees first. But whether a methane exceedance shows up in it depends on how each permit is written. Under the federal rule, an exceedance that is corrected on schedule is not a violation.61 Some New York permits still require it to be reported as a deviation; others don’t. The detailed surface data sits in appendices, and the federal electronic reporting system doesn’t reliably capture it either.

Why it matters: When the summary says “no deviations,” the patterns described in this report (the same locations failing quarter after quarter, readings in the hundreds of thousands of ppm, 120-day deadlines extended) disappear from view unless someone reads every appendix. Few reviewers can do that across dozens of landfills, and the public can’t do it at all without a records request.

What we found in New York: Two landfills in the same DEC region, monitored by the same consultant under the same federal rule, report the same kind of event differently. Seneca Meadows’ permit requires corrected exceedances to be reported “as deviations,” and its 2024 compliance certification marks the surface methane condition “Y.”62 Mill Seat’s report for the first half of 2025 has no row for surface methane and states that “there were no permit deviations identified during this reporting period” meaning that… Its own appendices show 58 locations over the federal limit in those two quarters, a reading of 335,485 ppm, nine locations sent to the 120-day list, and extension requests for nine of 16 Q4 2024 locations.63

The federal record has gaps of its own. In its January 2025 report, High Acres’ operator told EPA that the agency’s electronic reporting form “does not correctly calculate the number of exceedances due to an error in the formula,” is capped at 476 rows, and has “no place to add the concentration value.”64 The operator flagged the problem in writing; the form it described is the one every landfill must use.

At Modern Landfill, nine months after EPA’s scans found leaks at one in five points, DEC reviewed the operator’s quarterly reports and found “no significant issues.”65 Its air permit expired in 2013 and has been extended ever since.66

And at Brookhaven, the Town certifies compliance with its flare performance condition using a 2004 stack test of a flare that has since been disconnected (Section 5).67

The fix: The model rule moves beyond paper compliance in three ways.68 First, it makes the information public: a one-stop page for each landfill showing surface monitoring results, exceedances, corrective actions, which parts of the landfill were and weren’t monitored, gas collection downtime, destruction efficiency, and enforcement actions. California’s 2025 rule already requires a public data platform that updates as operators submit new information.69 Second, it requires real-time public notification when exceedances or major emission events occur. Third, it gives regulators clear authority and tools to act on what the data shows. For New York, the record also has to be consistent: every surface exceedance should be reported as a deviation under every permit, whether or not it was corrected on time; surface data should include all readings and every 120-day listing, extension and alternative remedy, with repeat locations flagged; and DEC should not accept reporting formats, state or federal, that cannot record the concentration of an exceedance.

7. Underground Landfill Fires: The Warning Limits New York Lets Operators Loosen

The Problem: When waste buried deep inside a landfill becomes unusually hot, it can lead to an underground fire. These are more like chemical reactions than regular house fires, and are incredibly difficult to control once established. Underground landfill fires have happened around the country, from Chiquita Canyon in California to Countywide in Ohio, and the federal rules, which New York follows, are built to catch them late, not prevent them.

Today’s federal rules allow 145°F as the trigger for action, but landfill operators can win approval to run even hotter, or with more oxygen getting in, without ever explaining the root cause. Federal rules also rely on wellhead readings that can be more than 120°F off from the temperature inside the waste. While unusually high temperatures don’t automatically indicate a fire, they should be taken seriously, investigated thoroughly, and quickly mitigated

Why it Matters: People living near landfills with subsurface elevated temperature events can lose their homes, their health, and sometimes their livelihoods. One particularly heartbreaking example is the community of Val Verde, California, which is home to the notoriously noxious Chiquita Canyon Landfill, operated by Waste Connections, where an underground chemical reaction has been raging, spewing toxic air emissions and geysers of toxic leachate. Nearby residents have been begging policymakers for relief for years, sharing their harrowing experiences with asthma attacks, nosebleeds, vomiting, miscarriages, and cancer.

What we found in New York:

  • New York approved a troubling oxygen amount. Landfills are designed to operate without oxygen. When oxygen shows up in a gas well, it usually means air is being pulled into the waste through cracked cover, erosion, settlement, or too much vacuum on the wells. That matters because oxygen is a key ingredient in subsurface fires and elevated-temperature events. It also inhibits the methane-forming microbes that a gas collection system relies on. Despite this, in December 2017, High Acres asked DEC to raise the oxygen limit from 5% to 20% at eight gas wells "to improve the overall gas collection efficiency in the wells and to provide odor control," and proposed that readings between 5% and 20% would "not be tracked by the site as deviations."70 Ordinary air is about 21 percent oxygen. DEC approved it for nine wells in a one-page letter; the only oxygen condition is that if levels exceed 20%, the facility "will inform the Department and re-evaluate”71

  • New York approved higher than normal temperature while warning signs flashed: EPA flags methane levels below 40% as an indicator of a landfill running too hot, yet High Acres landfill’s request for a higher operating temperature shows seven of the eight wells dropping below 40% methane. At one well, methane fell from 66.4% to 15.1% in about four months as oxygen rose from zero to 13.2%; at another it fell from 68.9% to 14.8% with oxygen at 17.7%. Remember, High Acres is the landfill where neighbors logged 4,604 odor complaints in 2020 alone.72

The fix: New York should take a page from the Ohio EPA, which shows what a real review looks like. Its June 2026 guidance for landfills seeking a higher temperature limit asks the question New York never did: why is this well hot? Before any approval, the operator must submit a root cause analysis and show it has already tried to fix the problem. It must also describe the well’s construction, the cover and any subsidence, surface emissions data, the age and type of waste, any heat-producing waste such as aluminum waste or ash, leachate recirculation, liquid levels, and whether a camera inspection was done. It must submit trend graphs of temperature, pressure, methane, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide, with at least one carbon monoxide sample if none exists. And it must document a physical check for flames, smoke, steam, odors, rapid settlement, or char. The new limit can’t exceed the measured maximum by more than 10°F, doesn’t take effect until the Ohio EPA approves it in writing, and comes with conditions that trigger re-evaluation. It is guidance, not law, so states should write it into rule.

New York should also add the rest of California’s fire-prevention toolkit on top of that. Continuous wellhead monitoring would catch over-pulling that draws in air. Continuous downwell temperature monitoring would show what the wellhead can’t: at Chiquita Canyon, a well reading 141°F at the surface was 188°F forty feet down. Monthly gas readings would trigger a root cause analysis when they shift. Escalating action thresholds would start at 131°F and tighten oxygen limits as temperature rises. And leachate recirculation should stop, since at the Countywide landfill in Ohio it set off a heat-producing reaction in aluminum waste.

Conclusion

New York can’t afford to wait. DEC put amendments to cut landfill greenhouse gas emissions on its 2026 regulatory agenda, and its own stakeholder presentation in June found that landfills produce 78 percent of the waste sector’s emissions. DEC has since proposed new rules for landfill leachate but the draft methane rule has yet to appear. Every quarter it waits is another quarter of the leaks documented in this report.

The evidence is in DEC’s own files. A landfill that burned nearly a billion cubic feet of gas in a year was never required to check its surface for leaks. Another slipped back under the federal threshold with a sample taken a month before EPA found it over. New areas of waste went five years without a single leak check, then turned up readings as high as 82 times the limit the first time anyone looked. The same leaks came back quarter after quarter, while regulators could require nothing more than another scan. Large parts of some landfills went unchecked, and EPA inspectors found 20 leaks at one landfill that the operator’s own survey had missed. Flares were certified on paper, or on a test of equipment that’s no longer connected. And one compliance report claimed “no permit deviations” while its own appendices showed 58 locations over the federal limit, one of them at more than 670 times the limit.

None of this required anyone to break the rules. It is what the federal floor allows. That is why California, Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Maryland and Michigan have built their own rules on top of it.. Roughly 372 landfills already meet tougher state standards, while communities from Seneca Falls to North Bellport keep breathing the cost of New York’s delay.

DEC should issue a draft rule now, and that rule should:

  • Rule applicability and thresholds: Outdated thresholds exempt many smaller but high-emitting landfills, concentrating uncontrolled emissions in surrounding neighborhoods. Expanding coverage closes this loophole and prevents communities from bearing the health burden of unregulated methane and associated air toxics.

  • Gas Collection and Control System (GCCS) design, installation, and expansion: Methane and hazardous co-pollutants are released almost immediately after waste is buried, yet federal rules delay gas collection for years. Earlier installation and continuous expansion into all areas of the waste mass prevent avoidable pollution during the most emission-intensive phase of landfill operation.

  • GCCS operation, control devices, and fire prevention: Poorly operated or weakly maintained systems leak gas, increase fire risk, and expose workers and nearby residents to harmful emissions. Stronger operational, efficiency, and maintenance standards protect both public health and site safety while delivering real emissions reductions.

  • Energy projects: Clear standards are needed to ensure these systems actually reduce pollution rather than masking ongoing exposure.

  • Landfill cover management: Landfill cover practices fail communities when methane and co-pollutants leak through cracks

  • Methane monitoring, reporting, and enforcement: Increased coverage and frequency of monitoring, use of modern and effective detection technologies, paired with public transparency and enforceable corrective action are essential to protect communities and ensure emissions reductions are real.

New York has the records, the authority and a rulemaking underway. The rule it writes should make sure the next set of records shows not just what the federal floor requires, but what is actually coming out of the ground.

Methods for Section 4

Purpose. This appendix explains how each figure in Section 4 was produced, so it can be checked against the source documents. All sources are operator reports submitted to DEC or EPA and obtained through FOIL, or EPA correspondence.

1. Seneca Meadows: share of grid squares walked. Source: GHD quarterly Surface Monitoring reports, Q1 2022 through Q3 2025 (15 reports). Tables 1–6 of each report list, by landfill section, every grid square monitored with its grid ID, date, time and reading. Procedure: we extracted the text of each report and collected every grid ID with a reading in each quarter. The reference set is every grid ID with a reading in at least one of the 15 quarters (1,583 squares). For each quarter, squares skipped = reference set minus squares with a reading. Because the reference set contains only squares walked at least once, the result is a floor: areas never walked in any quarter, such as most of Northwest Expansion Stage 5, are not counted. Checks: no grid ID repeats within a section in a quarter; adding Q3 2025 did not change the reference set. Limitation: the reports do not state a total grid count, and grid size (about 100 feet, from the stated 30-meter traverse) should be confirmed from the Surface Monitoring Plan before any acreage is stated.

2. Mill Seat and High Acres: area of shaded exclusion zones. Source: Figure 1 of each GHD quarterly report, an 11 × 17 inch sheet at a stated scale of 1 inch = 400 feet, with exclusion zones shaded in legend colors (Mill Seat: green, “area not yet subject to surface monitoring (waste < 5 years old)”; orange, “active / unsafe to traverse”. High Acres: purple, “not yet subject to NSPS monitoring”; orange, “unsafe to traverse”). Procedure: each figure page was converted to an image at 100 dots per inch (one pixel = 4 × 4 feet; 2,722.5 pixels per acre); pixels matching each legend color were grouped into zones, patches under about 1.1 acres (labels and markers) were discarded, and overlapping zones were counted once. Scale check: High Acres grid squares measure about 98 feet on a side at this scale. Each quarter’s zones were checked visually against the source map. Denominators: Mill Seat 216.9-acre permitted footprint (Monroe County); High Acres 234.1 acres constructed of a 320.4-acre approved footprint (WM, Q2 2024). Limitations: measurements are within a few acres; High Acres Q1 2023 was measured from a lower-resolution copy; Mill Seat’s 2022 maps show no shaded zones and are not included; only shaded zones are counted.

3. Broome County: points not monitored. Source: Broome County semiannual NSPS/NESHAP report, January–June 2023, Appendix A, SCS Field Services Q2 2023 report (June 27, 2023), Table 1, Old Landfill/Section I route, points 1–514. Procedure: we counted the points recorded as “NA Area not monitored, Active construction area” by parsing the table text: 272 of 514. The count was confirmed twice, by hand and by script.

4. Seneca Meadows: never-walked non-NSPS area. Source: GHD Q3 2023 report, Figure 5 (Northwest Expansion Grid Locations), hatched area labeled “NON-NSPS AREA.” Procedure: the hatched area was identified from its diagonal line pattern and measured in pixels, then divided by the average grid-square area on the same figure. The result, about 120–135 squares, is an estimate and is labeled as one.

5. Independent inspections. High Acres: EPA’s audit locations (WM close-out letter, Oct. 26, 2023: 22 locations) were compared by location ID with every location GHD’s Q2 2023 report lists above 200 ppm (37 locations); two IDs appear in both. Seneca Meadows: EPA’s 20 readings above 500 ppm are listed on pp. 3–4 of GHD’s Q3 2023 report; 11 carry Northwest Expansion IDs. A separate table in the same report (Table 9) lists eight readings EPA took above the surface at wellhead connections and a blower flange; these are component leaks, not surface exceedances, and are not used in Section 4.

6. Reproducibility. Every figure in Section 4 can be checked from the cited documents without our code, by counting table rows or measuring map areas at the stated scale. The extraction scripts, per-quarter grid lists for Seneca, and measurement overlays for each map are kept with the project files and can be shared on request.
